Batch GD is very slow
Stochastic GD
* Makes algorithms much faster
* Makes it possible to train on huge training sets
* However, it is much less regular than BGD
* Cost function will bounce up and down, decreasing only on average

* Due to stochastic (random) nature, SGD could bounce around and never reach the minimum.
* A remedy is to reduce the learning rate over time
* Start with large steps towards the minimum and gradually reduce it as you get closer to the minimum.
* This process is called simulated annealing
* A function, commonly used function, called learning schedule, can be used for this task
Mini-batch GD
* Uses a small batch of random instances at each iteration
* Performance boost from hardware optimization of matrix operations, especially when using GPUs
* Progress in parameter space is less erratic than SGD

Cross-Validation
* What if you don't have lots of data to split between train and validation sets

* Split the training set into complementary subsets
* Train the model using a different combination of these subsets and validate the model against the remaining parts
* Once hyperparameters are selected
* Train the model on the full training set
* Measure the generalization error on the test set
* Set aside some of the data for tests. The rest is for training and validation

* Put the rest of the data into sets with folds
* Set 1: Training: [1,2,3,4], Validation: [5]
* Set 2: Training: [1,2,3,5], Validation: [4]
* Set 3: Training: [1,2,4,5], Validation: [3]
* Set 4: Training: [1,3,4,5], Validation: [2]
* Set 5: Training: [2,3,4,5], Validation: [1]
* Take the average of the performance measures from the sets
* If not happy with the average, change the hyperparameters and try again
* If happy, use all the folds to train the model using the same parameters, then apply the final model on the test set that we put aside
* Loop (model, scores) then predict

Ridge regression - L2 Norm
Adds the following regularization term to the cost function
* This will keep the model parameters small
* α (regularization parameter) will be between 0 and 1
* α controls the amount of shrinkage applied to the coefficients during the regression process
* Large α will over-regularize and may lead to bias
* High α means high regularization - the weights are going to be smaller
* Lower α means low regularization - the weights are going to be bigger
* You don't want to use a very high value for alpha, close to underfitting, loses flexibility
Lasso Regression - L1 Norm
Same as ridge, except it uses l1 norm
* Important characteristics
* It tends to completely eliminate the weights of the least important features (i.e., set to zero)
* Meaning: automatically performs feature selection and outputs a sparse model
* Not as sensitive to outliers as Ridge

CH 4
Chapter 4 — The Abstraction: The Process (Quick Summary)
* Goal/Crux: Give users the illusion of many CPUs on a machine with few by virtualizing the CPU. The OS does this via time sharing (rapidly switching between processes); the tradeoff is potential slowdown when sharing.
* Mechanisms vs. Policies:
* Mechanisms = how (e.g., context switch: save/restore registers to stop one process and run another).
* Policies = which/when (e.g., scheduler chooses the next process using history, workload type, and performance goals).
* Keep them separate to swap policies without reworking mechanisms.
* What is a Process?
A running program with a machine state consisting of:
* Address space (code, static data, heap, stack)
* CPU registers (incl. PC/IP and SP, plus others)
* I/O state (e.g., open files)
* Process API (typical OS calls):
* Create a process
* Destroy (kill) a process
* Wait for a process to finish
* Control (suspend/resume)
* Status (query state, runtime, etc.)
* How a Program Becomes a Process:
* Load code & static data from disk/SSD into memory (often lazily).
* Set up stack (incl. argc/argv for main()).
* Initialize heap (grows via malloc()).
* Set up I/O (e.g., UNIX default stdin/stdout/stderr).
* Transfer control to the program’s entry point (main()).
* Process States & Transitions:
* Running (on CPU), Ready (runnable but not running), Blocked (waiting on I/O/event).
* OS schedules Ready→Running and deschedules Running→Ready.

* I/O completion typically moves Blocked→Ready; scheduler decides if it runs immediately.
* OS Data Structures:
* Process List of all processes; each has a PCB (Process Control Block) with:
* Register context (for context switches)
* State, PID, parent
* Open files, cwd, kernel stack, etc.
* Extra states like embryo (creating) and zombie (exited, not yet reaped; parent can wait() to collect status).
* Time vs. Space Sharing (tip):
* Time sharing: slice a resource over time (CPU, network link).
* Space sharing: divide the resource spatially (disk blocks).
CH 5
Interlude — Process API (Chapter 5) — Quick Summary
* Core idea: UNIX creates and controls processes with three pillars: fork(), exec(), and wait().
* fork() — make a new process
* Duplicates the calling process (parent) to create a child with its own PID and (logically) its own address space.
* Return values differ: parent gets child’s PID; child gets 0; negative means failure.
* After fork(), both parent and child continue from the next instruction—execution order is non-deterministic (scheduler decides).
* wait() / waitpid() — synchronize with children
* Parent blocks until a child finishes; returns the child PID (and optionally exit status).
* Makes output sequences deterministic when you need the child to finish before the parent proceeds.
* exec() family — replace the current program

* Loads a new executable into the current process (no new PID), replacing code, data, stack/heap setup, then does not return on success.
* Variants (execl, execv, execvp, etc.) differ in how you pass args/env and whether PATH is searched.
* Why split fork() and exec()? (Shell superpower)
* The shell does: fork() → (child sets up environment: redirection, pipes, env vars, cwd, signals) → exec() → parent wait()s.
* This separation enables:
* Redirection: child closes STDOUT_FILENO, opens a file → program’s prints go to that file.
* Pipes: connect one process’s stdout to another’s stdin via pipe() to build command chains.
* Open file descriptors & exec
* FDs remain open across exec() (unless marked close-on-exec), which is why redirection and pipes keep working after the exec.
* Users, signals, and control
* Signals (e.g., SIGINT via Ctrl-C, SIGTSTP via Ctrl-Z) let you interrupt/stop processes; processes can handle signals.
* Users can control their own processes; root (superuser) can control any process—use sparingly.
* Handy tools: ps, top, kill, killall.
* Key takeaways / vocab
* PID: numeric process ID.
* Parent/child: relationship formed by fork().
* Non-determinism: post-fork() scheduling order isn’t guaranteed.
* PCB / process state details live with the OS (from prior chapter), but this interlude focuses on the API surface.
* Homework themes
* Observe copy-on-write behavior with variables across fork().
* Share/use FDs across parent/child; concurrent writes.

* Make child print before parent (e.g., with wait() or other sync).
* Try all exec* variants; use wait() vs waitpid().
* Practice redirection and pipe() to connect two children.

AgriSciences is a data solutions company that has a vision of providing sustainable nutrition for everyone. Their main goal is to empower producers to reach their goals by creating data-driven services and technology.

After spending countless hours applying to internships and refining my resume to match the job descriptions for internships throughout the country, I secured this internship through a recommendation from Professor Varghese. The week before finals, Professor Varghese sent me an email about an open summer internship position at AgriSciences. I quickly responded to the email saying I would be interested in the position, and Professor Varghese sent them a recommendation. That day, I applied on their website, and a few days later, I received a text from an unknown number saying that he was from AgriSciences and that he would like to interview me for their open position. I met with Jason and Greg, the co-founders of AgriSciences, at a Starbucks the next day for an interview. I showed them how I could help their business, along with some of my relevant school projects that I have worked on throughout my collegiate career. By the time the interview was over, they told me that they would like to hire me for their open intern position.
The role of my position contributed to creating reports with accurate data for our clients.

I had a few weekly and monthly tasks that I was in charge of doing. I had to retrieve some of our clients’ weekly data from an external source, format the data accordingly, and upload it to the client's database. Those were the basics of the weekly and monthly tasks, but I had some bigger projects that I worked on over the summer. I was tasked with helping create workflows and Python notebooks to extract user, authorization, summary, and interval data from an API put together by an electric company based in California. This data would end up being used to show the client how much energy they have used and what type of energy is being used, whether it is gas, electric, or solar. The end goal for this task was to create dashboards with easy-to-understand visualizations so that the client can view everything about their energy usage. I enjoyed working on this project because I could see the progress being made after each item on the task list was completed, rather than working towards some never-ending goal. Another item I was tasked to work on was to create and map fields in an agriculture management software, which helps farmers see where and what they need to plant.

My internship experience correlated with the work I did in my courses at UWRF in a few different ways. The first major part was working with databases, writing SQL queries, and visualizing trends in the data. I learned a lot of these skills in CIDS 333, Database Management. CIDS 333 taught me how a typical database stores its data and how a query is a simple way to shrink all the data down to what you need. In my time working, I had to write queries to see if there were duplicate rows or if there was any missing information in the tables. I learned a lot from my classes at UWRF, but I also learned just as many things during my internship. Along with using SQL, I used a lot of Python during my time at AgriSciences. I never actually took a class that taught me Python, but I learned the basics in Java and C, which helped me transition over to using Python on the job.

Throughout my internship, I learned many things and accomplished a multitude of goals. I learned how to use a Microsoft application called Power BI. Power BI is a useful tool to create dashboards that contain graphs, charts, tables, and more in order to help visualize your data. I have used Power BI to create reports for clients so that they can see their fuel usage more clearly. The reports show a graph for each location of their fuel stations and a meter to indicate if they are running low on fuel. Another thing I learned was how to create a flow on Power Automate. A flow triggers from an HTTP request. The flow can then run scripts, create tables or rows in a database, send emails, and much more. I used flows in one of my projects that were triggered whenever a new client authorized their account with us. The flow would then trigger and start retrieving customer data based on the new user's subscription ID. Apart from learning things, I also accomplished a goal of mine. The goal was to land an internship after months of applying, and I am thankful to Dr. Varghese for recommending me for the position.

Communication, professionalism, and critical thinking were some of the Career Readiness Competencies that I was able to further develop in my time as an intern. I grew in my communication skills because, as a remote worker, I would have to reach out to my coworkers if I were having trouble in a certain area, since not being in an office together, they are not able to see my struggles. Every task for a project that I would complete, I would let a coworker know so that they could either review my work or add onto what I was doing. Through communication on Microsoft Teams and constant emails, I learned that the more questions I ask, the better. My coworkers were there to help me succeed, and all I had to do was ask for help if I needed it. Sometimes I would have to communicate in a very professional manner when requesting something from a client. I learned the best ways to send a professional email from being CC’d in my coworkers' emails to clients. Along with professional emails, I learned that dressing up in clothes that look presentable helps me act more professional in the workplace. Even though I did not put too much thought into my outfit, I would have to think hard about what could be the best way to go about solving a problem. I gained critical thinking skills by combining my school knowledge with the knowledge I was gaining every day at work. My favorite idea I came up with this summer was optimizing a database operation for one of our tables. I realized that since new data was being added each day, instead of reuploading the entire table to the database, we could apply a date signature column and create a composite primary key based on the data and another column that was in the table.

I learned a lot of stuff from the work we did at AgriSciences, but I also learned a few things about myself. I realized that I can push myself at work to meet deadlines and ensure that a quality product is sent. In high school, I used to cut corners to get something done as quickly as possible. Now that I have gained some real-life and work experience, I know the importance of efficiency and quality time. The better something is done the first time, the less time needed to go back and fix anything you may have missed. Working at AgriSciences has shown me what I am capable of doing in a professional environment.
This internship has solidified my choice of being a computer science student. I now know that I can graduate in December, knowing I made the right degree choice. I am still very interested in the field of computer science. This internship has shown me what someone in my major could expect it to be like working in the professional world. I enjoyed working in teams to solve problems. I also liked not being on my feet all day like jobs I have had in the past. I have learned a lot this summer, and I hope to learn even more in my professional career.

I would recommend this position to any UWRF computer science student who is looking for an internship position for many reasons. Being part of a company with only four other people, I was able to communicate with all of them and hear their feedback daily. The work I did as an intern was a great learning experience for someone entering the professional field because I had a great team to explain the tasks and also help me wherever I got stuck. Overall, it was a great work environment for my first white collar job. Overall, working at AgriSciences over the summer has taught me how I can apply the knowledge that I have gained from my classes in the professional world.
